b: Inside a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility, Eva Yi Xie managed to find a book to read for her thesis project.

The facility has a library, and while browsing the catalog, Xie found a book on cognitive ecology, says her mentor, Carlos Brody, professor of neuroscience at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute. She hasn’t been able to get a copy yet, but she is “very eager” to read it, Brody says.

Xie, a Chinese-born graduate student at Princeton University, has been held in ICE custody since 19 November. U.S. immigration officials apprehended her at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, near Washington, D.C., as she was traveling from the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting.

Xie spent her first two nights in custody in a Chantilly, Virginia, detention center, where she slept on a paper sheet on the floor, Brody says. By Saturday morning, she had been moved to the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia. She now has a bed and access to showers, video calls and the library.

Through video calls, Xie has been “trying to take care of things back home,” Brody says. She has tasked friends with looking after her boyfriend, says Xie’s friend of six years, who spoke with her via video call on Sunday. The friend requested anonymity due to privacy concerns. Xie has also asked about her active projects and checked to ensure her lab animals are being cared for, Brody says.

In addition to trying to get a copy of the cognitive ecology book, Xie has spent time practicing her Spanish with other detained people, the friend says. “She’s holding out strong in the face of this.”

esterday, Xie made a video call to Brody while he was at lunch with members of the three labs that she is involved with, Brody says. All of the attendees were able to see her and talk to her. “She did show off her blue inmate jumpsuit, and she was being funny about it, but it was also heartbreaking,” Brody says.

Xie’s friends and colleagues created a website to share updates on the situation and provide ways to help, such as signing a petition for Xie’s release and contacting senators. Yesterday afternoon, local and student organizations hosted a rally on the Princeton campus advocating for Xie’s release. About 250 people attended, including New Jersey state senator Andrew Zwicker, The Daily Princetonian reported.
“It’s been pretty remarkable to see how much capacity our community has for organizing,” says Julie Charlton, a visiting postdoctoral research associate in Brody’s lab.

On Friday, Xie’s lawyers filed a petition challenging the legality of her detention. In response, a judge barred ICE from moving Xie out of Virginia and ordered the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to respond to the petition by 5 p.m. on 25 November. Xie’s lawyer, Kerry Doyle, was not available to provide a comment to The Transmitter ahead of this article’s publication.

In a recent video call, Xie expressed her gratitude for everyone who has been working toward her release, Charlton says. “What Eva said was that it was gratitude beyond what either English or Chinese could express.”
